section_summary: This section consists chiefly of Peruvian press clippings from October 1937 debating Japanese immigration, landholding, employment, small business, and colonization. Most articles express strongly anti-Japanese and often explicitly racist fears about economic displacement, demographic change, espionage, and national sovereignty, while H. Ikeyama defends the Japanese community’s commercial and agricultural activities. Other pieces discuss immigration enforcement at Callao and the Perú Takushoku Kumiai agricultural settlement in Chanchamayo.

subfiles.title: La Inmigración Asiática y el Mejoramiento de la Raza
subfiles.about: An explicitly racialist argument for restricting Asian immigration while encouraging selected European and North American settlement in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Olivares links ancient American civilizations to prehistoric Asian migration but depicts modern Asian immigration as a threat to Peru’s racial composition, economy, public health, and sovereignty. He invokes heredity theories and Japanese birth statistics in Lima, advocates European and North American colonization, and warns that continued Japanese penetration could reduce Peru to a colony of the Mikado.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa: La Colonia Japonesa—El Pequeño Comercio y la Pequeña Industria IV
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 37 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.about: An analysis of Japanese participation in Peru’s small businesses and trades and of governmental measures limiting foreign economic activity.
subfiles.summary: The article argues that Japanese migrants left agriculture for cities and increasingly dominated cafés, bakeries, barbering, retailing, and several manual trades, sometimes displacing Chinese as well as Peruvian operators. It cites business-license statistics, the immigration report of Toru Ogishima, and Peru’s decree of June 26, 1936 concerning immigration quotas, foreign registries, national labor percentages, business transfers, and yanaconaje. The author presents legal restriction as necessary to protect Peruvians and prevent a future conflict with the Japanese community.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 38 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.from: Jorge Badani, President of the Asociación Rural del Perú
subfiles.about: An argument that high rents and superior Japanese cooperative credit were transferring coastal farmland from Peruvian to Japanese cultivators.
subfiles.summary: Badani attributes Japanese agricultural expansion to landowners’ demands for high rents and entrance payments and to the favorable financing available through the Central Japonesa. He contrasts this cooperative system with expensive, collateral-heavy Peruvian credit and argues that it gives Japanese beginners a decisive advantage. He calls for reform of the Banco Agrícola, protection of Peruvian cultivators, regulation of land leases, and closer control of credit and foreign cultivation.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa: Se siente en el ambiente la pauperización y desplazamiento de brazos que origina la inmigración japonesa
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 39 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.about: A demand to halt Japanese immigration on the grounds that it displaced Peruvian labor and preserved a separate Japanese national identity.
subfiles.summary: Figueros San Miguel claims Japanese businesses evade labor laws, pay very low wages, and displace both Peruvian capital and workers. He argues that Japanese schools in Lima inculcate loyalty to Japan and that Peru-born Japanese graduates might enter Peru’s professional and governing classes while remaining committed to Japan. He cites alleged Japanese efforts to consolidate control over land in the Tulumayo area of Huánuco.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa: Un punto sobre cada i—Nuevos conceptos sobre los mismos errores
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 40 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.from: H. Ikeyama, Director of Perú Jiho
subfiles.to: Guillermo Salinas Cossío and La Prensa readers
subfiles.about: Ikeyama answers Salinas Cossío’s allegations concerning Japanese trade, agricultural activity, diplomacy, remittances, and population in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Ikeyama denies that Japan’s pursuit of free trade amounts to dumping or commercial hegemony and uses 1936 production and export figures to dispute the claim that Japan exported 60 percent of its output. He clarifies that he credited Japanese immigrants with improving cotton yields rather than creating superior cotton fiber, for which he acknowledges Fermín Tangüis. He maintains an estimate of 23,000 Japanese immigrants pending a national census and promises a Spanish-language section in Perú Jiho to encourage Peruvian-Japanese understanding.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa: Esta discusión no es de figuras literarias, sino de vida o muerte para el Perú
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 41 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.to: H. Ikeyama and La Prensa readers
subfiles.about: A rebuttal to Ikeyama assembling claims that Japanese residents were gaining control of land, commerce, transportation, and institutions in Peru.
subfiles.summary: Zegarra cites correspondents from Huaral, Chancay, Barranca, and Iquitos to argue that Japanese ownership and networks excluded Peruvians from farming, commerce, professions, and transportation. He invokes Carlos Enrique Paz Soldán’s demographic arguments and claims that Japanese schools, newspapers, high birth rates, and remittances threatened Peruvian nationality and economic independence. The article urges enforcement of immigration quotas and official surveillance of Japanese educational, commercial, journalistic, and social institutions.

subfiles.title: La Inmigración Asiática en el Perú
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 42 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.from: Semana, reporting an interview with Rivera Schreiber
subfiles.about: A brief report on Peruvian enforcement of immigration law against passengers arriving from the Far East.
subfiles.summary: Rivera Schreiber states that a Foreign Relations commission functions regularly and sends a member to inspect each vessel arriving from the Far East. Few Japanese or Chinese passengers are now admitted, and several travelers on the two most recent ships were returned at the shipping company’s expense because their passports were not satisfactory.

subfiles.title: El Peligro Amarillo en América: El Japón pretende absorber nuestras industrias y comercio—La democracia de América en peligro
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 43 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.about: An alarmist article portraying Japanese migration, commerce, and alleged espionage as part of an imperial plan for domination of the Pacific and South America.
subfiles.summary: The article alleges that Japan seeks control of the Pacific and operates espionage networks in the United States and around the Panama Canal. It portrays South American republics as targets for Japan’s excess population and describes Peru as the first likely victim because of Japanese positions in agriculture, commerce, and industry. Its argument relies heavily on racial hierarchy and a comparison with British rule in India; the installment ends with “Continuará.”

subfiles.title: El Chisme del Día: Filantropía Asiática
subfiles.doc_type: Satirical newspaper column; Enclosure No. 44 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.about: A sarcastic attack on Ikeyama’s claim that Japanese enterprises such as Perú Takushoku Kumiai advanced Peru’s prosperity without seeking profit.
subfiles.summary: The columnist mockingly calls Japanese economic activity “philanthropy” while alleging that Japanese operators displaced Peruvian tenant farmers and workers, violated employment-percentage laws, and attempted to bribe officials. The piece specifically invokes the Chancay Valley and accuses Japanese employers of reserving skilled work for their compatriots.

subfiles.title: La Infiltración Japonesa: Desde el Comercio Minorista Hasta las Empresas Colonizadoras de la Montaña
subfiles.doc_type: Newspaper clipping; Enclosure No. 45 to despatch No. 245
subfiles.from: H. Ikeyama, Director of Perú Jiho
subfiles.to: Guillermo Salinas Cossío and La Prensa readers
subfiles.about: Ikeyama defends Japanese participation in urban trades and explains the cooperative agricultural settlement established by Perú Takushoku Kumiai in Chanchamayo.
subfiles.summary: Ikeyama contends that Japanese merchants generally acquired businesses from Chinese, Italian, and other foreign operators rather than displacing Peruvians, and he disputes Salinas Cossío’s bakery figures. He says efforts to recruit Peruvian barbers drew few applicants. He describes Perú Takushoku Kumiai, founded in 1931, as a nonprofit experimental colony on 1,000 hectares in Chanchamayo, where twenty Japanese families cultivated coffee and maize to demonstrate methods potentially useful to Peru and later settlers.
